newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco trial could begin by Labor Day - attorneys.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco trial could begin by Labor Day - attorneys.

text.p: Attorneys involved in Florida's $1 billion tobacco trial agreed Thursday that testimony could get under way by Labor Day on September 1.
"That is possible. It is do-able," said Robert Montgomery, the Florida attorney charged with helping choose the six-member jury and nine alternates in the first state Medicaid case to come to trial.
"The way the judge has things set up now that is a very reasonable date," Montgomery said during a break in the screening of Palm Beach County residents for jury service.
Murray Garnick, an attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc., agreed with Montgomery's Labor Day prediction for a starting date.
"We should be done by then," he said, adding "We (the tobacco companies) have been ready for this trial for months."

Florida is suing for what it spent to treat nicotine- addicted Medicaid patients between the years 1994 and 1996. The suit is based on passage in 1994 of Florida's Third-Party Medicaid Law which allows the state to recover what it spent to care for these patients.
It is also seeking triple damages based on charges which allege that the tobacco companies used false advertising to lure new and young non-smokers to their products.

Florida also wants punitive damages under provisions of Florida's racketeering statute. Under it, they have accused the tobacco companies of allegedly joining together for the purpose of hiding the truth about the dangers of smoking from the public, the Congress and various regulatory agencies.

Montgomery's prediction followed Palm Beach County Circuit Court Judge Harold Cohen's setting out his formula for securing the jury and alternates for the case. With the ease with which attorneys have been finding potential jury candidates, Cohen said, they could expect to begin challenges by August 18.

A potential juror can be dropped if he voices strong opinions, or has a strong belief, that would interfere with his or her ability to decide the case solely on the law as given by the judge and the evidence presented by the attorneys through documents and witnesses.

Under Cohen's plan, the initial screening of potential jurors will be completed by August. 18. On that date, the first 50 prospective jurors will be brought in for interrogation by attorneys for Florida and the tobacco companies. Each side will have a half-day to question them.
At the end of the day, attorneys for both sides will announce their challenges for cause, Cohen said. Those left will be asked to return for the final screening that will begin August 25.
Cohen said the same procedure will be followed with the remaining 75 potential jurors. The only difference is that they will be screened at the rate of 25 each day.
He urged attorneys to be judicious in their use of preemptory challenges, where they do not have to state reasons why they want the potential candidate to be off the jury.
"Don't use them all up or we wil all be back again (to trying to find potential jurors," Cohen said.
